los.text: Identify the key issues and subtypes of dementia
los.html:
• Dementia: progressive, acquired decline in memory and other cognitive domains (language, executive function, visuospatial, attention, behaviour) sufficient to impair daily function, without clouding of consciousness. ~900,000 in UK
    • prevalence doubles every 5 years after 65.
Subtype%Key features
Alzheimer's disease~60%
  • Insidious, progressive episodic memory loss (recent events), then language (word-finding), visuospatial, executive
  • Early hippocampal involvement
  • Risk: age, APOE ε4, Down syndrome
Vascular dementia~15–20%Stepwise decline, vascular risk factors/strokes, executive dysfunction, slowed processing, focal signs, gait disturbance, mood change; MRI white matter disease/infarcts
Mixed (AD + vascular)Common
Dementia with Lewy bodies~10–15%Fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder, parkinsonism; severe neuroleptic sensitivity; attention/visuospatial > memory early
Parkinson's disease dementiaDementia >1 year after established PD motor symptoms
Frontotemporal dementia~2–5% (younger, 45–65)Behavioural variant (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsions, hyperorality) or language variants (semantic, non-fluent PPA); memory relatively preserved early
Others/reversible mimicsAlcohol-related (Korsakoff), normal pressure hydrocephalus (gait, incontinence, dementia), CJD (rapid, myoclonus), HIV, B12/thyroid deficiency, depression ("pseudodementia"), delirium, subdural haematoma, tumours
Key issues
  • Diagnosis (often late/missed)
  • Capacity and decision-making
  • Risk (driving, wandering, finances, cooking, falls, self-neglect, abuse)
  • Carer stress
  • Behavioural and psychological symptoms (BPSD)
  • Delirium susceptibility
  • Comorbidity/polypharmacy
  • End-of-life planning
  • Stigma
  • Cost of care.
Mild cognitive impairment (MCI)Cognitive decline greater than expected for age but function preserved; ~10–15%/year progress to dementia.

los.text: Describe how to assess memory loss and cognition
los.html:
History(patient and informant)
  • Onset (gradual vs sudden)
  • Progression (gradual vs stepwise)
  • Domains affected (memory: repeating questions, misplacing items, getting lost; language; executive; visuospatial; behaviour/personality)
  • Impact on ADLs/IADLs (finances, medications, cooking, driving)
  • Mood
  • Psychotic symptoms
  • Sleep (RBD)
  • Falls/parkinsonism
  • Vascular risk factors
  • Alcohol
  • Drugs (anticholinergic burden, sedatives)
  • FHx
  • Education/occupation
  • Hearing/vision.
ExaminationNeurological (focal signs, parkinsonism, gait, primitive reflexes), cardiovascular (AF, BP), signs of alcohol excess, thyroid, hearing/vision.
Cognitive testingACE-III (100 points; domains), MoCA (30), Mini-Cog, 6CIT and GPCOG (primary care); MMSE (copyrighted, less used).
Delirium screen4AT (alertness, AMT4, attention (months backwards), acute change/fluctuation).
Exclude reversible causes (bloods)FBC, U&E, LFT, calcium, glucose/HbA1c, TFTs, B12 and folate, ± syphilis/HIV serology (risk), CRP, urine (if delirium).
Imaging
  • CT or MRI brain (atrophy pattern: hippocampal (AD), frontotemporal; vascular changes; exclude tumour, subdural, NPH)
  • DaTSCAN (DLB), FDG-PET/SPECT
  • CSF amyloid/tau or amyloid PET in specialist settings.
ReferralMemory assessment service (diagnosis, subtype, post-diagnostic support).

los.text: Describe how to formulate a management plan for patients with dementia
los.html:
• Person-centred, MDT plan:
    • Diagnosis disclosure and information (patient and carers), post-diagnostic support (dementia support worker, Alzheimer's Society).
    • AChEIs (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): mild–moderate AD; also DLB and Parkinson's dementia.
    • Memantine: moderate AD if AChEI not tolerated, severe AD, or add-on.
    • Not for vascular dementia (unless mixed) or FTD. Review anticholinergic burden and sedatives.
    • Non-drug: cognitive stimulation therapy (mild–moderate), cognitive rehabilitation, reminiscence therapy, exercise, music/art, sleep hygiene, sensory aids (hearing aids, glasses).
    • Manage comorbidities and vascular risk (BP, diabetes, smoking, statins, AF anticoagulation).
    • BPSD (behavioural and psychological symptoms): look for triggers first (pain, infection, constipation, environment, unmet needs).
    • Non-drug first: person-centred care, structured activities, DICE approach.
    • Antipsychotics only for severe distress/risk: risperidone, short term, lowest dose, review at 6 weeks. ↑ stroke and death. Avoid in DLB.
    • Treat depression: SSRIs, mirtazapine.
    • Risk and safety: driving (DVLA), home safety (OT assessment, assistive technology, telecare), medication management (blister packs), finances (LPA, scams), wandering, falls, safeguarding.
    • Legal/advance planning: Lasting Power of Attorney (health and welfare; property and finance), advance care planning, advance decisions, wills while capacity remains; capacity assessments (MCA).
    • Carer support: carer's assessment, respite, education, support groups, benefits (Attendance Allowance).
    • Social care: care packages, day centres, care homes when needed.
    • End-of-life care: recognising advanced dementia, avoiding burdensome interventions (PEG), palliative care.

los.text: Describe the key issues and subtypes of dementia and how to assess memory loss and cognition
los.html:
Summary combining LO 1 and 2
  • Key issues: progressive cognitive and functional decline; diagnostic uncertainty (MCI vs dementia vs depression vs delirium); subtype affects prognosis and treatment (e.g. avoid antipsychotics in DLB; AChEIs not for vascular/FTD); capacity, risk, carer burden, BPSD, comorbidity, ethical issues (autonomy vs safety).
  • Subtypes: Alzheimer's (memory first, insidious), vascular (stepwise, vascular risk), Lewy body (fluctuations, hallucinations, parkinsonism, RBD), frontotemporal (behaviour/language, younger), mixed, reversible causes.
  • Assessment: informant history, cognitive tests (ACE-III/MoCA), functional assessment (ADLs/IADLs, OT), mood screen (depression: GDS), delirium screen (4AT), physical exam, bloods (reversible causes), neuroimaging, specialist memory clinic.
ACE-III interpretation
  • <82–88/100 suggests impairment (cut-off 88 sensitive, 82 specific)
  • Domain profile helps subtype (e.g. low memory/fluency in AD; low fluency/language in FTD; visuospatial low in DLB).
Differentiating dementia, delirium and depression
DementiaDeliriumDepression
OnsetInsidiousAcute (hours–days)Weeks–months
CourseProgressiveFluctuatingPersistent, diurnal
AttentionNormal earlyImpairedUsually normal
ConsciousnessClearAlteredClear
Effort on testingTries, confabulatesVariable"Don't know" answers

los.text: Describe how the process of neurodegeneration links to changes in memory.
los.html:
Memory systems
  • Episodic (events; hippocampus, medial temporal lobe, entorhinal cortex, Papez circuit)
  • Semantic (facts; anterior temporal lobes)
  • Working memory (prefrontal cortex)
  • Procedural (skills; basal ganglia, cerebellum).
Memory formation
  • Encoding → consolidation (hippocampus, long-term potentiation (LTP) via NMDA receptors, synaptic plasticity; sleep) → storage (neocortex) → retrieval.
  • Cholinergic input (basal forebrain: nucleus basalis of Meynert, medial septum) supports attention and encoding.
Neurodegeneration → memory change
  • Alzheimer's: amyloid-β aggregation (oligomers impair LTP/synapses; plaques) → tau hyperphosphorylation → neurofibrillary tangles, spreading in a predictable sequence (Braak stages): transentorhinal/entorhinal cortex → hippocampus (early episodic memory loss: can't form new memories, forgets recent events; remote memories preserved initially) → association neocortex (language, visuospatial, executive) → primary cortices late. Synaptic loss correlates best with cognitive decline. Loss of cholinergic neurons (nucleus basalis) → basis for AChEI therapy. Glutamate excitotoxicity → memantine.
  • Frontotemporal: frontal/anterior temporal lobes → behaviour and semantic memory loss, episodic memory relatively spared.
  • Lewy body: cortical and brainstem α-synuclein, cholinergic deficits → attention, visuospatial; fluctuations.
  • Vascular: subcortical white matter disruption of frontal–subcortical circuits → slowed processing, executive, retrieval problems.
  • Korsakoff: thiamine deficiency → mammillary bodies/thalamus → anterograde amnesia, confabulation.

los.text: Identify the key pathological features of different neurodegenerative diseases.
los.html:
DiseaseKey pathological features
Alzheimer's disease
  • Macroscopic: generalised cortical atrophy (hippocampal/medial temporal, parietal), widened sulci, hydrocephalus ex vacuo.
  • Microscopic: extracellular amyloid-β (neuritic) plaques (Aβ42 from APP cleavage by β- and γ-secretase)
  • Intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau; silver stain)
  • Neuronal and synaptic loss
  • Granulovacuolar degeneration
  • Hirano bodies
  • Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (lobar haemorrhages).
  • Genetics: APP, PSEN1/2 (early-onset AD), APOE ε4 (risk), trisomy 21
Dementia with Lewy bodies / Parkinson's diseaseLewy bodies: intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions of α-synuclein (± ubiquitin) in cortex (DLB) and substantia nigra (PD: pallor/loss of pigmented neurons)
Frontotemporal lobar degeneration
  • Knife-edge atrophy of frontal/temporal lobes
  • Inclusions of tau (incl. Pick bodies: round tau inclusions), TDP-43 (often with MND, C9orf72), or FUS
Vascular dementiaMultiple infarcts, lacunes, white matter ischaemic change (small vessel disease: arteriolosclerosis), microbleeds
Huntington's diseaseCaudate (and putamen) atrophy → enlarged lateral ventricles ("boxcar"), CAG repeat in HTT, huntingtin aggregates
Prion disease (CJD)Spongiform change (vacuoles), neuronal loss, gliosis, PrPˢᶜ deposits (florid plaques in vCJD); no inflammation
MND (ALS)Loss of upper (motor cortex: Betz cells) and lower (anterior horn) motor neurons, TDP-43 inclusions, Bunina bodies; SOD1, C9orf72
Multiple system atrophy / PSPα-synuclein glial inclusions / tau (midbrain atrophy: "hummingbird sign")
  • Common themes: protein misfolding and aggregation (proteinopathies), selective neuronal vulnerability, spread (prion-like), gliosis (astrocytes, microglia), neuronal loss/atrophy.

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to treat dementia and delirium and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
Dementia drugs

DrugMechanismUse / evidenceSide effects / cautions
Donepezil, rivastigmine (oral/patch), galantamineAcetylcholinesterase inhibitors → ↑ synaptic AChMild–moderate AD, DLB, PDD: modest benefit on cognition, function, behaviour (delays decline ~6–12 months); not disease-modifyingBradycardia, heart block, syncope (check ECG/pulse), GI (nausea, diarrhoea), vivid dreams/insomnia, urinary incontinence, ↑ gastric acid (PUD), bronchospasm
MemantineNMDA receptor antagonist (↓ glutamate excitotoxicity)Moderate–severe AD; add-onDizziness, headache, constipation, ↓ dose in renal impairment
Anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab)Remove amyloid plaquesModest slowing in early AD; MHRA-licensed but not recommended by NICE for NHS use (cost–benefit)ARIA (oedema/microhaemorrhage), infusion reactions; APOE ε4 risk
  • Avoid/deprescribe: anticholinergics (oxybutynin, amitriptyline, chlorphenamine), sedatives
    • antipsychotics only for severe BPSD with risk (risperidone short-term; ↑ stroke and mortality; contraindicated/dangerous in DLB/PDD → neuroleptic sensitivity).

Delirium

  • Treat the cause (infection, drugs, dehydration, pain, urinary retention, constipation, hypoxia, metabolic, alcohol withdrawal) + non-drug measures (reorientation, glasses/hearing aids, familiar people, sleep, mobilisation, hydration, avoid moves/catheters/restraint).
  • Drugs only if severely distressed or a risk to self/others and de-escalation fails. Review daily, stop ASAP.
DrugWhenCautions
Low-dose haloperidol (e.g. 0.5 mg)First choice, short termCheck QTc; avoid in Parkinson's/DLB
LorazepamAlcohol withdrawal, Parkinson's/DLB, antipsychotics contraindicatedCan worsen delirium
  • Alcohol withdrawal delirium: chlordiazepoxide (reducing regimen) + Pabrinex.

los.text: Understand the implications of the Human Rights Act for medical practice
sessions: MHS: Human Rights Act in Medical Practice
los.html:
Human Rights Act 1998
  • Incorporates the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law (from 2000).
  • Public authorities (NHS bodies, doctors employed by them, care homes providing public services, local authorities) must act compatibly with Convention rights
  • Individuals can bring claims in UK courts
  • Courts interpret legislation compatibly.
Types of rightsAbsolute (cannot be limited: Art. 3), limited (Art. 5), qualified (can be interfered with if lawful, necessary and proportionate for legitimate aim: Arts 8, 9, 10).
ArticleRightMedical relevance
2Right to lifeDuty to protect life (suicide risk in detained patients: Rabone 2012), resuscitation decisions (DNACPR must involve patient/family: Tracey 2014), no right to assisted dying (Pretty)
3Prohibition of torture, inhuman or degrading treatmentNeglect, restraint, dignity in care, conditions of detention, force-feeding
5Right to liberty and securityDetention under Mental Health Act, Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (Bournewood, Cheshire West 2014 "acid test"), restraint
6Fair hearingTribunals, disciplinary processes
8Respect for private and family lifeConsent (bodily integrity), confidentiality, access to records, family visits, end-of-life choices, reproductive decisions
9Freedom of thought, conscience and religionReligious beliefs (Jehovah's Witnesses), conscientious objection
10Freedom of expressionWhistleblowing
12Right to marry and found a familyFertility treatment
14Prohibition of discrimination (with other rights)Equal access to treatment (age, disability, race)
  • Implications for practice: respect autonomy and dignity, proportionate restrictions, involve patients/families in decisions, document reasoning, follow MCA/MHA safeguards.

los.text: Analyse the psychological, sociological, and biological influences on ageing. Describe psychological and sociological explanations for the course of mental health challenges in later life.
sessions: MHS: Perspectives on ageing and mental health
los.html:
Biological influences on ageing
  • Cellular senescence
  • Telomere shortening
  • Accumulated DNA damage
  • Oxidative stress
  • Mitochondrial dysfunction
  • Chronic low-grade inflammation ("inflammageing")
  • ↓ physiological reserve (homeostenosis)
  • Sensory decline
  • Sarcopenia
  • Multimorbidity
  • Brain changes (atrophy, ↓ processing speed; crystallised intelligence preserved vs fluid intelligence declines).
Psychological influences
  • Personality stability
  • Coping and resilience
  • Sense of control and purpose
  • Adaptation to losses (Baltes: selective optimisation with compensation)
  • Erikson's final stage: integrity vs despair
  • Cognitive reserve (education)
  • Attitudes to ageing (positive self-perceptions → longer life: Levy).
Sociological influences
  • Disengagement theory (mutual withdrawal; criticised) vs activity theory (staying active promotes wellbeing) vs continuity theory
  • Structured dependency (retirement, pensions create dependence)
  • Ageism
  • Social isolation and loneliness (bereavement, retirement, mobility), poverty, caring roles, social networks, cultural roles of older people
  • "third age" vs "fourth age".
Mental health in later life
  • Depression: common (~10–15% community, more in care homes/hospital), under-recognised (somatic presentation, "normal ageing" assumption), linked to physical illness, pain, disability, bereavement, isolation, loss of role; high suicide risk in older men.
  • Psychological explanations: learned helplessness, loss and grief, cognitive distortions, reduced reinforcement (behavioural); sociological: loss of status/role, isolation, poverty, institutionalisation, ageism.
  • Also anxiety, late-onset psychosis, alcohol misuse, dementia-related symptoms.
CourseMay be chronic/relapsing; physical comorbidity and cognitive impairment worsen outcome; good response to treatment is possible (CBT, antidepressants, social prescribing).

los.text: Describe the challenges of patients with dementia as well as by their carers, and how to deliver person-centered care.
sessions: Challenges and dilemmas in dementia care
los.html:
Challenges for patients
  • Memory loss and disorientation
  • Loss of independence/identity/roles
  • Communication difficulties
  • BPSD (agitation, aggression, wandering, apathy, psychosis, sleep disturbance)
  • Depression/anxiety
  • Stigma
  • Vulnerability to abuse/scams
  • Falls
  • Malnutrition
  • Incontinence
  • Pain (under-recognised)
  • Delirium with acute illness
  • Hospital admissions (disorientation, deconditioning)
  • Decisions about moving to care homes
  • Loss of capacity.
Challenges for carers
  • High carer burden (physical, emotional, financial)
  • Depression/anxiety
  • Isolation
  • Guilt
  • Grief ("ambiguous loss")
  • Sleep deprivation
  • Managing behaviours
  • Navigating services/funding
  • Legal decisions (LPA)
  • Own health problems (often elderly spouses)
  • Young carers.
Person-centred care(Kitwood)
  • See the person, not the disease; maintain personhood; VIPS framework: Value people, Individualised care, Perspective of the person, Social environment.
  • Know the person's life story ("This is Me" document), preferences, routines, values.
  • Communication: simple sentences, one question at a time, non-verbal cues, patience, validation (rather than confrontation/reality orientation), avoid "elderspeak".
  • John's Campaign (carers' right to stay with patient in hospital), dementia-friendly wards (signage, colour contrast, clocks), avoid unnecessary moves, meaningful activity, involve carers in decisions, support carers (respite, carer's assessment), advance care planning, best-interests decisions under MCA.

los.text: Identify possible differential diagnoses and holistic management options for a patient presenting with memory loss.
los.html:
Differential diagnosis of memory loss
  • Neurodegenerative dementias: Alzheimer's, vascular, mixed, Lewy body, frontotemporal, Parkinson's dementia.
  • MCI, normal age-related forgetfulness, subjective cognitive decline.
  • Delirium (acute, fluctuating; superimposed on dementia).
  • Depression ("pseudodementia") and anxiety.
  • Reversible/medical: hypothyroidism, B12/folate deficiency, hypercalcaemia, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, medications (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids, antiepileptics), alcohol (Korsakoff, alcohol-related brain damage), normal pressure hydrocephalus, chronic subdural haematoma, brain tumour, infections (HIV, syphilis, encephalitis), OSA, sensory impairment (hearing loss), transient global amnesia, epilepsy (transient epileptic amnesia), CJD (rapid), autoimmune encephalitis.
Holistic management options
  • Biopsychosocial: medical (treat cause, drugs for AD/DLB, manage comorbidities, deprescribing)
  • Psychological (CST, CBT for depression/anxiety, post-diagnostic counselling)
  • Social (care packages, day centres, carers' support, financial/legal planning, LPA, benefits, housing adaptations, assistive tech)
  • Functional (OT, physiotherapy, falls prevention)
  • Safety and risk (driving, wandering, fire/gas)
  • Advance care planning
  • Involve MDT (memory clinic, GP, community mental health team for older adults, social services, third sector).

los.text: Elicit a third-party history of cognitive decline, ensuring relevant information about cognitive changes, functional abilities, and behaviours is gathered
sessions: Memory problems and risk history and assessment
los.html:
Informant (collateral) historySomeone who knows the patient well (spouse, child, carer); with patient's consent where possible; consider seeing informant separately (frank discussion).
Cognitive changes
  • When first noticed, onset (sudden vs gradual), progression (gradual, stepwise, fluctuating, rapid), examples:
  • Memory: repeating questions/stories, forgetting appointments/conversations, misplacing items, forgetting names, getting lost in familiar places.
  • Language: word-finding difficulty, reduced speech, comprehension problems.
  • Executive: planning, organising, problem solving, managing finances/bills, multitasking.
  • Visuospatial: driving problems, getting lost, difficulty dressing/judging distances.
  • Attention/orientation: fluctuation, confusion about time/place.
Functional abilitiesIADLs (shopping, cooking, finances, medications, telephone, transport, driving) usually affected first; then basic ADLs (washing, dressing, eating, toileting, continence, mobility).
Behaviour/psychologyPersonality change, disinhibition, apathy, irritability/aggression, low mood, anxiety, hallucinations (visual: DLB), delusions (theft), sleep disturbance (RBD: acting out dreams), wandering, eating changes.
Other
  • Falls
  • Incontinence
  • Gait change
  • Parkinsonism
  • Vascular events
  • Alcohol
  • Drugs
  • FHx
  • Hearing/vision
  • Carer stress and support
  • Safety concerns (cooking, wandering, scams, driving, firearms)
  • Legal arrangements (LPA).

los.text: Administer the ACE-III (Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination) and interpret the results to assess cognitive impairment
sessions: Memory problems and risk history and assessment
los.html:
ACE-III (Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination III)
  • ~15–20 min
  • 100 points across 5 domains: Attention (18) (orientation, serial 7s/registration)
  • Memory (26) (recall, name and address learning and delayed recall, famous people)
  • Fluency (14) (letter P words, animals in 1 min)
  • Language (26) (comprehension, writing, repetition, naming, reading)
  • Visuospatial (16) (overlapping pentagons, wire cube, clock drawing, counting dots, fragmented letters).
Administration
  • Quiet room
  • Check hearing aids/glasses
  • Explain purpose
  • Consent
  • Standardised instructions and timing
  • Don't prompt beyond instructions
  • Record verbatim
  • Account for education level, language, sensory impairment, mood
  • Use the scoring guide.
Interpretation
  • Cut-offs: ≤88 (sensitive, ~94%) and ≤82 (specific, ~100%) suggest dementia in validation studies; scores should be interpreted with history and function (not diagnostic alone).
  • Domain profile: AD → low memory (delayed recall) and orientation; FTD (bvFTD) → low fluency, language (semantic variant: naming/comprehension), memory relatively preserved; DLB/PDD → low attention, visuospatial (pentagons, cube), fluency; vascular → attention/fluency (executive, processing speed).
  • Serial testing for progression.
LimitationsEducation/cultural bias, non-native English speakers, low literacy, sensory/motor impairment, depression/anxiety, delirium (invalid).

los.text: Formulate a comprehensive risk assessment for a patient with dementia, considering cognitive, functional, and safety aspects of care
sessions: Memory problems and risk history and assessment
los.html:
Risk domains
  • Cognitive: forgetting to eat/drink/take medicines (missed or double doses), getting lost/wandering, poor judgement (scams, financial abuse), inability to recognise danger.
  • Functional: falls (gait, environment, postural hypotension, drugs), cooking (fire, gas left on), personal care/hygiene, continence, nutrition/hydration.
  • Safety: driving (DVLA must be informed: assessment), fire/gas/electricity, flooding, smoking, firearms, access to medications, living alone, self-neglect, exploitation/abuse (safeguarding), risk to others (e.g. caring for dependent person, aggression).
  • Medical: comorbidities, delirium risk, polypharmacy, swallowing (aspiration), pain.
  • Psychological: depression, suicide risk, psychosis, agitation/aggression.
  • Social: carer strain/breakdown, isolation, finances, housing.
Formulate
  • Identify each risk, its likelihood and severity, protective factors, the person's wishes and capacity (positive risk-taking: balance autonomy and safety; unwise decisions are allowed if capacitous), least restrictive interventions (pill organisers/blister packs, telecare (falls pendant, smoke/gas detectors, GPS trackers), meals on wheels, carers, day centres, OT home adaptations, cooker cut-offs, LPA, safeguarding referral), and review plan
  • Document and share with MDT/carers.

los.text: Perform whole spine assessment examination to screen for common abnormalities and recognise red flags requiring further assessment and investigation.
sessions: MSK Whole spine assessment and introduction to clinical reasoning
los.html:
Whole spine screen (GALS-based + spinal exam)
  • Look: from behind, side and front: posture, scoliosis, kyphosis (thoracic), lumbar lordosis, muscle wasting, asymmetry, skin (café-au-lait, hairy patch, scars), shoulder/pelvic levels.
  • Feel: spinous processes and paraspinal muscles for tenderness, step deformity (spondylolisthesis), sacroiliac joints.
  • Move: cervical (flexion, extension, lateral flexion, rotation), thoracic (rotation sitting), lumbar (flexion: modified Schober's test (<5 cm increase: ankylosing spondylitis), extension, lateral flexion); straight leg raise (sciatic nerve stretch: L5/S1), femoral stretch test (L2–L4), neurological exam of limbs (myotomes, dermatomes, reflexes), gait.
Red flags for serious spinal pathology(urgent investigation, e.g. MRI)
  • Cauda equina syndrome: saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction (retention, incontinence), sexual dysfunction, bilateral sciatica/leg weakness → emergency MRI.
  • Malignancy: history of cancer, age >50, weight loss, night pain/unremitting pain, thoracic pain.
  • Infection (discitis, epidural abscess): fever, IVDU, immunosuppression, recent infection.
  • Fracture: trauma, osteoporosis, steroid use, older age.
  • Inflammatory (axial spondyloarthritis): <40, insidious onset, morning stiffness >30 min, improves with exercise, night pain (second half), alternating buttock pain.
  • Progressive neurological deficit, myelopathy signs (UMN), structural deformity, AAA (pulsatile mass).

los.text: Evaluate presenting clinical information to select the most appropriate physical assessment and perform structured shoulder or knee examination.
sessions: MSK Whole spine assessment and introduction to clinical reasoning
los.html:
• Select exam from presentation: joint pain localisation, mechanism (trauma, overuse), age, referred pain (neck → shoulder; hip → knee).

Shoulder examination

LookSymmetry, wasting (supraspinatus/infraspinatus fossae, deltoid), scars, swelling, deformity (ACJ step, winging of scapula).
FeelSCJ, clavicle, ACJ, acromion, greater tuberosity, bicipital groove, scapula, temperature.
Move
  • Active then passive: flexion, extension, abduction (painful arc 60–120° = impingement/rotator cuff; 140–180° = ACJ)
  • Adduction
  • External rotation (↓ passive ER = frozen shoulder, OA)
  • Internal rotation (hand behind back).
Special tests
  • Rotator cuff power (supraspinatus: empty can/Jobe's; infraspinatus/teres minor: resisted ER; subscapularis: lift-off/belly press)
  • Impingement (Hawkins–Kennedy, Neer's)
  • Biceps (Speed's)
  • Apprehension/relocation (instability)
  • Scarf test (ACJ).
  • Examine neck.

Knee examination

LookStanding (varus/valgus, wasting of quadriceps, swelling, Baker's cyst), gait, lying (scars, effusion, redness).
FeelTemperature, effusion (patellar tap, sweep test), joint line tenderness (meniscus), patella, tibial tuberosity, popliteal fossa.
MoveFlexion/extension (active, passive), crepitus, fixed flexion, straight leg raise (extensor mechanism).
Special tests
  • ACL (anterior drawer, Lachman's: most sensitive)
  • PCL (posterior sag, posterior drawer)
  • Collaterals (valgus stress: MCL; varus: LCL, at 0° and 30°)
  • Menisci (McMurray's, Thessaly)
  • Patellar apprehension.
  • Examine hip (referred pain).

los.text: Analyse clinical findings in the context of anatomical knowledge to identify potential underlying pathologies affecting the shoulder or knee.
sessions: MSK Whole spine assessment and introduction to clinical reasoning
los.html:
FindingLikely pathology
Painful arc 60–120°, pain over lateral deltoid, positive Hawkins/JobeSubacromial impingement / rotator cuff tendinopathy (supraspinatus under acromion/coracoacromial arch)
Weakness of abduction/ER, can't initiate abduction, drop-arm signRotator cuff tear
Global ↓ active and passive ROM, especially external rotation, normal X-ray, diabetesAdhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)
↓ ER + crepitus, olderGlenohumeral OA
ACJ tenderness, high painful arc, positive scarf testACJ arthritis/injury
Apprehension on abduction/ER, previous dislocationAnterior instability (Bankart lesion: anterior labrum)
Shoulder pain with neck pain, dermatomal symptomsCervical radiculopathy (C5/6)
Twisting injury, rapid effusion (<2 h: haemarthrosis), pop, instability, +LachmanACL rupture (± meniscal tear, MCL: "unhappy triad")
Twisting, delayed swelling (next day), joint line tenderness, locking, +McMurrayMeniscal tear (medial commoner)
Valgus injury, medial pain, laxity on valgus stressMCL sprain/tear
Dashboard injury, posterior sagPCL injury
Anterior knee pain on stairs/sitting, youngPatellofemoral pain
Older, crepitus, varus deformity, bony swelling, ↓ ROMKnee OA
Hot swollen joint, feverSeptic arthritis/crystal arthropathy → aspirate
  • Anatomical reasoning: identify structure under the tender point, the movement that stresses it, and mechanism of injury.

los.text: Formulate an appropriate plan for further investigation or referral, based on clinical findings and current guidelines.
sessions: MSK Whole spine assessment and introduction to clinical reasoning
los.html:
Investigations
  • X-ray (2 views): fractures, OA, calcific tendinitis, dislocation; weight-bearing knee X-ray for OA. Ottawa knee rules for trauma.
  • USS: rotator cuff tears, bursitis, effusions, guided injections.
  • MRI: ligament/meniscal tears (ACL, menisci), labral tears (MR arthrogram), red flags, persistent symptoms, pre-surgery.
  • Bloods: CRP/ESR, FBC, urate, RF/anti-CCP if inflammatory; joint aspiration if hot swollen joint.
Management/referral (guideline-based)
  • Conservative first for most: analgesia (topical/oral NSAIDs), activity modification, physiotherapy (rotator cuff, patellofemoral, OA: NICE: exercise + weight loss), steroid injection (subacromial, frozen shoulder).
  • Urgent referral: acute traumatic rotator cuff tear in younger patients (repair within weeks), unreduced dislocation, locked knee (bucket-handle meniscal tear), ACL rupture in active patient (orthopaedics/sports clinic), fractures, suspected septic arthritis (same day), tumour/red flags, neurovascular compromise.
  • Routine orthopaedic referral: persistent symptoms after conservative care, mechanical symptoms, instability, severe OA affecting quality of life (joint replacement).
  • Rheumatology referral for inflammatory arthritis (urgent).

los.text: Clearly and concisely present clinical findings from a musculoskeletal examination using appropriate medical terminology and structure.
sessions: MSK Whole spine assessment and introduction to clinical reasoning
los.html:
Structure"I examined Mr X's right knee. On inspection ... On palpation ... Movement ... Special tests ... In summary ..."
Example (knee)
  • "On inspection in standing there was mild valgus alignment with quadriceps wasting on the right.
  • Lying, there was a moderate effusion with no erythema or scars.
  • The knee was warm with a positive patellar tap and medial joint line tenderness.
  • Range of movement was 5–110° actively and passively, limited by pain.
  • Collateral ligaments were stable; anterior drawer and Lachman's were negative; McMurray's was positive medially with a palpable click.
  • The hip was normal.
  • In summary, the findings suggest a medial meniscal tear.
  • I would arrange an MRI and refer to physiotherapy/orthopaedics."
TerminologyEffusion (small/moderate/large), crepitus, fixed flexion deformity, varus/valgus, range in degrees, MRC power, named special tests (positive/negative), laterality (right/left; medial/lateral).
TipsPresent positive findings first, mention relevant negatives (neurovascular status, joint above/below), give a diagnosis/differential and plan.

los.text: Identify normal intracranial and spinal anatomy on CT and MRI, including ventricles, CSF spaces, and major brain structures
los.html:
CT basics
  • Density in Hounsfield units (HU): air −1000 (black)
  • Fat −100
  • Water/CSF 0
  • Brain grey matter ~40
  • White matter ~30
  • Acute blood ~60–80
  • Bone +1000 (white)
  • Window settings (brain, subdural/blood, bone windows).
Normal anatomy to identify on CT/MRI
  • Ventricles: lateral ventricles (frontal horns, bodies, occipital and temporal horns), 3rd ventricle (midline slit between thalami), cerebral aqueduct, 4th ventricle (posterior fossa, in front of cerebellum).
  • CSF spaces: sulci, Sylvian (lateral) fissures, basal cisterns (suprasellar, ambient, quadrigeminal, perimesencephalic: effacement = raised ICP/herniation), cisterna magna.
  • Brain structures: grey–white matter differentiation, basal ganglia (caudate head beside frontal horn, lentiform nucleus), internal capsule, thalami, corpus callosum, frontal/parietal/temporal/occipital lobes, brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla), cerebellum, falx cerebri, tentorium, pineal (often calcified), choroid plexus (calcified).
  • Skull/bones: vault, skull base, sinuses, mastoid air cells (bone window).
MRI
  • T1 (CSF dark, fat bright; anatomy)
  • T2/FLAIR (CSF bright on T2, suppressed on FLAIR; oedema/white matter lesions bright)
  • DWI (acute infarct bright with low ADC within minutes)
  • SWI/GRE (blood, microbleeds)
  • Gadolinium (BBB breakdown: tumours, abscess, active MS).
Spine MRIVertebral bodies, discs, spinal cord (terminates ~L1–L2 as conus), CSF around cord, cauda equina, nerve roots, epidural space.

los.text: Describe the radiological appearances of key acute intracranial pathologies such as intracerebral, subdural, extradural, and subarachnoid haemorrhage, as well as acute infarcts
los.html:
PathologyCT appearance
Extradural haematoma
  • Biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense collection, doesn't cross sutures (dura attached at sutures), may cross midline/tentorium
  • Usually temporal, with skull fracture (middle meningeal artery)
Subdural haematoma
  • Crescent-shaped, follows brain contour, crosses sutures but not the midline (falx)
  • Bridging vein tear (elderly, alcohol, anticoagulants, infants/abusive head trauma)
  • Acute hyperdense, chronic hypodense
Subarachnoid haemorrhage
  • Hyperdense blood in basal cisterns, Sylvian fissures, sulci ("star"/pentagon)
  • ± hydrocephalus
  • CT sensitivity ~100% within 6 h of thunderclap headache (LP for xanthochromia ≥12 h if CT negative later)
Intracerebral haemorrhageHyperdense parenchymal haematoma (hypertensive: basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum; lobar: amyloid angiopathy, AVM, tumour) ± oedema, intraventricular extension
Acute ischaemic infarct
  • Early (<6 h): often normal CT
  • Subtle signs: loss of grey–white differentiation (insular ribbon sign, obscured lentiform nucleus), sulcal effacement, hyperdense MCA sign (clot)
  • Later (>24 h): wedge-shaped hypodensity in vascular territory
  • MRI DWI positive within minutes
  • CT angiography/perfusion: large vessel occlusion (thrombectomy), penumbra.

los.text: Distinguish intra-cerebral from extra-cerebral abnormalities and recognise features such as mass effect, midline shift, and coning
los.html:
Intra-axial (intracerebral)
  • Arises within brain parenchyma: surrounded by brain tissue, expands the brain, gyral pattern displaced
  • e.g. gliomas, metastases, intracerebral haemorrhage, abscess, infarct.
Extra-axial (extracerebral)
  • Arises outside brain (meninges, skull, CSF spaces): broad base against dura/skull
  • Displaces brain inward with CSF cleft/vessels between lesion and cortex
  • "buckling" of grey–white junction
  • May cause bony change (hyperostosis)
  • e.g. meningioma (dural tail), extradural/subdural haematoma, schwannoma (CPA), epidermoid/arachnoid cyst.
Mass effect
  • Compression of adjacent structures: effacement of sulci
  • Compression of ventricles (ipsilateral)
  • Effacement of basal cisterns
  • Midline shift (septum pellucidum displaced >5 mm significant)
  • Hydrocephalus (obstruction of foramen of Monro/aqueduct/4th ventricle or trapped contralateral ventricle).
Herniation ("coning")
  • Subfalcine: cingulate gyrus under falx (anterior cerebral artery compression).
  • Transtentorial (uncal): medial temporal lobe (uncus) through tentorial notch → CN III compression (ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil), contralateral cerebral peduncle (Kernohan's notch: false localising), PCA compression, ↓ GCS.
  • Tonsillar ("coning"): cerebellar tonsils through foramen magnum → medulla compression → respiratory arrest, Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing).
  • Upward transtentorial (posterior fossa mass).
Signs on CTObliterated basal cisterns, low-lying tonsils, distorted brainstem.

los.text: Interpret CT and MRI features that differentiate acute, subacute, and chronic bleeds, and explain the relevance of density changes over time
los.html:
• Blood evolves with time on CT (as haemoglobin breaks down and clot retracts/resorbs):
PhaseTimeCT densityMRI (approximate)
Hyperacute/acuteHours–3 daysHyperdense (~60–80 HU) (bright white)T1 iso, T2 dark (deoxyHb)
Subacute~3 days–3 weeksIsodense to brain (~1–3 weeks): easily missed (look for mass effect, effaced sulci, displaced grey–white junction)T1 bright (methaemoglobin)
Chronic>3 weeksHypodense (darker than brain, approaching CSF)T2 bright fluid; haemosiderin rim dark on T2/SWI
Acute-on-chronic subduralMixed density with fluid–fluid level (hyperdense layer dependent), indicates re-bleeding.
Exceptions
  • Severe anaemia (Hb <80 g/L) → acute blood may look isodense
  • Active bleeding with unclotted blood ("swirl sign": hypodense areas within hyperdense haematoma → expansion risk)
  • Coagulopathy.
RelevanceEstimate timing of injury (e.g. safeguarding: subdurals of different ages in infants), guide management (chronic subdural: burr-hole drainage; acute: craniotomy), recognise isodense subacute subdural in elderly with insidious confusion.

los.text: Recognise the imaging features of common space-occupying lesions (e.g., metastases, primary brain tumours, abscesses) and spinal cord compression
los.html:
LesionImaging features
MetastasesMultiple, at grey–white junction, round, ring/solid enhancement, disproportionate vasogenic oedema; from lung, breast, melanoma (haemorrhagic), renal, colorectal
Glioblastoma (GBM)Solitary, irregular ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, surrounding oedema, crosses corpus callosum ("butterfly glioma")
Low-grade gliomaNon-enhancing T2/FLAIR hyperintense infiltrative lesion
MeningiomaExtra-axial, dural-based, homogeneous avid enhancement, dural tail, calcification, adjacent hyperostosis
Cerebral abscessSmooth thin ring enhancement, restricted diffusion centrally (DWI bright) (differentiates from necrotic tumour), oedema; source (sinus, ear, dental, endocarditis)
Vestibular schwannomaCPA mass extending into internal acoustic meatus ("ice cream cone")
LymphomaPeriventricular, homogeneously enhancing, restricted diffusion (HIV: ring-enhancing)
Toxoplasmosis (HIV)Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in basal ganglia
Spinal cord compression (MRI whole spine, T2 sagittal)
  • Vertebral body metastasis/collapse with epidural soft tissue compressing thecal sac/cord (loss of CSF around cord), cord signal change (oedema), multilevel disease
  • Also disc herniation, epidural abscess (enhancing collection, discitis), haematoma.
Next stepsContrast MRI, staging CT (primary), neurosurgery/oncology, dexamethasone for oedema.

los.text: Apply principles of clinical reasoning by integrating radiological findings with patient presentations (e.g., stroke vs haemorrhage, trauma vs coagulopathy)
los.html:
Integrate history, examination and imaging
  • Stroke vs haemorrhage: acute focal deficit; non-contrast CT first to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis; normal early CT doesn't exclude infarct; consider stroke mimics (hypoglycaemia, seizure/Todd's, migraine, tumour, functional).
  • Thunderclap headache: CT (SAH), then LP if negative after 6 h; CTA for aneurysm; consider RCVS, venous sinus thrombosis (CT venogram).
  • Trauma vs coagulopathy: on anticoagulants (warfarin/DOAC) even minor head injury → CT within 8 h (NICE); haemorrhage in unusual location/atraumatic → check clotting, platelets, liver disease; reverse anticoagulation urgently (PCC + vitamin K for warfarin; andexanet/idarucizumab).
  • Elderly with gradual confusion/falls → chronic subdural (isodense possible); young with focal seizure and fever → encephalitis/abscess (MRI, LP).
  • Headache with papilloedema → mass/IIH/venous thrombosis.
  • Known cancer with new neuro symptoms → metastases (MRI with contrast).
NICE head injury CT criteria (adults, within 1 h)
  • GCS <13 on initial assessment or <15 at 2 h
  • Suspected open/depressed skull fracture
  • Basal skull fracture signs (haemotympanum, panda eyes, CSF leak, Battle's sign)
  • Post-traumatic seizure
  • Focal deficit
  • >1 episode of vomiting.
AvoidAnchoring on imaging alone; correlate with clinical localisation.

los.text: Evaluate when imaging findings indicate urgent or life-threatening conditions that require immediate intervention (e.g., acute SAH, large extradural haematoma, cord compression)
los.html:
FindingWhy urgentImmediate action
Acute SAHRe-bleeding risk (highest in first 24 h), hydrocephalus, vasospasmNeurosurgery, CTA, nimodipine, BP control, coiling/clipping, EVD for hydrocephalus
Large extradural haematomaRapid deterioration ("lucid interval" then collapse), herniationEmergency craniotomy and evacuation (neurosurgery); airway protection
Acute subdural with mass effect/midline shiftHerniationNeurosurgery, reverse anticoagulation
Large ICH, posterior fossa haemorrhage/infarctBrainstem compression, hydrocephalusNeurosurgery (decompression/EVD), BP lowering, reversal
Signs of herniation (effaced cisterns, tonsillar descent), acute hydrocephalusImminent deathNeurosurgery (EVD), osmotherapy (mannitol/hypertonic saline), ICU, head up 30°, avoid hypercapnia
Acute ischaemic stroke with large vessel occlusionTime-critical ("time is brain")Thrombolysis (<4.5 h) / thrombectomy (up to 6–24 h selected)
Spinal cord compression/cauda equinaPermanent paralysis/incontinenceDexamethasone (MSCC), urgent spinal surgery/oncology (radiotherapy)
Cerebral abscess, venous sinus thrombosis, pneumocephalus/open fractureAntibiotics/neurosurgery; anticoagulation; antibiotics
  • Communicate urgently (critical result pathway), resuscitate (ABCDE), protect airway (GCS ≤8), monitor GCS/pupils.

los.text: Explain the clinical significance of neuro-imaging findings in guiding management decisions, such as eligibility for thrombolysis in stroke.
los.html:
Stroke thrombolysis decisions
  • Non-contrast CT excludes haemorrhage (absolute contraindication) and large established infarct (extensive early ischaemic change: ASPECTS score <6 → higher bleed risk, less benefit).
  • Alteplase/tenecteplase within 4.5 h of onset (last known well) if no haemorrhage and no other contraindications; MRI DWI–FLAIR mismatch can identify patients with unknown onset (wake-up stroke) within 4.5 h.
  • CT angiography identifies large vessel occlusion (ICA/M1/basilar) → mechanical thrombectomy (within 6 h; up to 24 h if CT perfusion/MRI shows salvageable penumbra).
Haemorrhagic stroke
  • Stop/reverse anticoagulants, intensive BP lowering (target SBP 130–140 within 1 h if SBP 150–220), neurosurgical referral (cerebellar, hydrocephalus)
  • CTA for underlying cause (aneurysm, AVM, spot sign).
Head injuryCT findings decide surgery (evacuation of EDH/SDH), ICP monitoring, observation, anticoagulant reversal.
SAHCT → CTA → aneurysm treatment (endovascular coiling preferred).
Tumours/abscessBiopsy/resection planning, steroids for oedema, antibiotics/drainage.
MSCC/cauda equinaMRI guides radiotherapy vs surgical decompression.
Secondary preventionImaging (carotid Doppler) → carotid endarterectomy if symptomatic stenosis ≥50–70% (NASCET) within 2 weeks.

los.text: Identify and describe the paths of the vertebral and internal carotid arteries.
los.html:
Internal carotid artery (ICA)
  • From common carotid bifurcation (C3/C4, upper border of thyroid cartilage)
  • → cervical part (no branches in neck; within carotid sheath with IJV and vagus)
  • → petrous part (carotid canal in temporal bone)
  • → over foramen lacerum
  • → cavernous part (within cavernous sinus, with CN VI; carotid siphon)
  • → cerebral part (pierces dura, gives ophthalmic artery, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal)
  • → terminates as anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
Vertebral artery
  • First branch of subclavian artery
  • → ascends through transverse foramina of C6 to C1
  • → winds around lateral mass of atlas (suboccipital triangle)
  • → foramen magnum
  • → runs on anterior medulla
  • → the two unite at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery.
  • Branches: posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) (lateral medulla, inferior cerebellum), anterior and posterior spinal arteries.
ClinicalCarotid stenosis/dissection (anterior circulation TIA/stroke, Horner's with dissection), vertebral artery dissection (neck manipulation, trauma: posterior circulation stroke, neck pain), subclavian steal (stenosis proximal to vertebral origin).

los.text: Identify the blood supply to the brain stem and cerebrum and link to the functional outcome of interruption of the blood supply in different arterial territories
los.html:
ArteryTerritoryOcclusion effects
Anterior cerebral (ACA)Medial frontal and parietal lobes (paracentral lobule)Contralateral leg > arm weakness/sensory loss, urinary incontinence, abulia/personality change
Middle cerebral (MCA)Lateral hemisphere (motor/sensory cortex for face/arm), internal capsule and basal ganglia (lenticulostriate branches), Broca/Wernicke (dominant)Contralateral face and arm > leg weakness/sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, aphasia (dominant, usually left) or neglect (non-dominant), gaze deviation towards lesion
Posterior cerebral (PCA)Occipital lobe, inferior temporal lobe, thalamusContralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, visual agnosia, memory problems, thalamic pain
Lenticulostriate (lacunar)Internal capsule, basal ganglia, thalamusPure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis, dysarthria-clumsy hand; no cortical signs
Vertebrobasilar (brainstem)Medulla, pons, midbrain, cerebellumCrossed signs (ipsilateral cranial nerve + contralateral limbs), vertigo, ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, ↓ consciousness
PICALateral medulla, inferior cerebellumLateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss + contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner's, ataxia, dysphagia/hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), vertigo, nystagmus
AICALateral pons, cerebellum, (labyrinthine artery)Lateral pontine syndrome: + ipsilateral facial palsy and deafness
Basilar occlusionPonsLocked-in syndrome (quadriplegia, preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements)
Paramedian midbrain (PCA branches)Weber's: ipsilateral III palsy + contralateral hemiplegia
  • Oxford (Bamford) classification: TACS (all 3: hemiparesis, homonymous hemianopia, higher cortical dysfunction), PACS (2 of 3), LACS, POCS.

los.text: Describe the distribution of the basilar artery to the pons, membranous labyrinth and cerebellum.
los.html:
Basilar artery
  • Formed by the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction.
  • Runs up the basilar groove on the anterior pons.
  • Ends at the upper border of the pons by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
Branches and distribution
  • Pontine arteries (paramedian and short/long circumferential): supply the pons (corticospinal tracts, cranial nerve nuclei V–VIII, medial lemniscus).
  • Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA): inferior anterior cerebellum, lateral pons; usually gives the labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery (sometimes directly from basilar) → membranous labyrinth (cochlea and vestibular apparatus) via the internal acoustic meatus: an end artery → occlusion → sudden deafness and vertigo.
  • Superior cerebellar artery (SCA): superior surface of cerebellum, upper pons/midbrain (CN III emerges between PCA and SCA: aneurysm compression).
  • Posterior cerebral arteries (terminal).
Cerebellum supplyPICA (from vertebral: inferior posterior), AICA (basilar: anterior inferior), SCA (basilar: superior).
ClinicalBasilar thrombosis (locked-in, coma; thrombectomy), "top of the basilar" syndrome (visual, oculomotor, memory, ↓ consciousness), vertigo/hearing loss from AICA/labyrinthine ischaemia (posterior circulation stroke mimicking peripheral vertigo: HINTS).

los.text: Identify all the components of the circle of Willis (circulus arteriosus) and make a labelled diagram of it.
los.html:
Circle of Willis (circulus arteriosus)Arterial anastomotic ring at the base of the brain surrounding the optic chiasm and pituitary stalk in the interpeduncular/suprasellar cistern.
Components
  • Anterior: two anterior cerebral arteries (A1 segments) joined by the anterior communicating artery (ACom).
  • Lateral: two internal carotid arteries (terminal parts) connected to the posterior circulation by the two posterior communicating arteries (PCom).
  • Posterior: two posterior cerebral arteries (P1) from the basilar artery bifurcation.
  • (MCAs arise from the ICAs but are not part of the ring.)
Labelled diagram (text version, viewed from below)
  • Top: ACA (left) — ACom — ACA (right)
  • Sides: ICA → (MCA branches laterally) → PCom running back to
  • Bottom: PCA (left) — basilar tip — PCA (right); basilar artery runs down to vertebral arteries.
FunctionCollateral flow if one inlet is occluded (variable; complete circle in only ~25–50% of people: hypoplastic segments common).
Clinical
  • Berry (saccular) aneurysms at branch points
  • Commonest at ACom (~35%)
  • PCom–ICA junction (→ painful CN III palsy with dilated pupil)
  • MCA bifurcation
  • Basilar tip → SAH.
  • Risk: ADPKD, Ehlers–Danlos, coarctation, smoking, hypertension, FHx.

los.text: Describe the course of the middle meningeal artery and explain the importance of its relationship to the skull bones and interior of the cranium
los.html:
• Middle meningeal artery (MMA): branch of the maxillary artery (first part, in infratemporal fossa)
    • → enters the skull through the foramen spinosum
    • → runs between the endosteal dura and the inner table of the skull (extradural position), dividing into anterior (frontal) and posterior (parietal) branches
    • grooves the inner skull.
  • Anterior branch passes deep to the pterion (H-shaped junction of frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones; thinnest part of the skull, ~3 cm above the zygomatic arch midpoint).
  • Importance: a blow to the side of the head/pterion
    • → temporal bone fracture
    • → tears the MMA
    • → arterial bleeding into the extradural space
    • → extradural haematoma (biconvex; limited by sutures where dura is tightly adherent)
    • → classic lucid interval then rapid deterioration (↑ ICP, uncal herniation: ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral hemiparesis)
    • → emergency craniotomy (burr hole at pterion in extremis).
  • Also supplies the dura and skull bones (most dural supply)
    • embolisation of MMA is now used to treat chronic subdural haematomas (recurrence prevention).

los.text: Identify the main structures involved in venous drainage of the brain and link to the symptoms and signs of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
los.html:
Venous drainage
  • Superficial cortical veins and deep veins (internal cerebral veins → great cerebral vein of Galen)
  • → dural venous sinuses (between endosteal and meningeal dura; valveless, no muscular walls)
  • → internal jugular veins.
Main sinuses
  • Superior sagittal sinus (along attached border of falx; receives CSF via arachnoid granulations)
  • → confluence of sinuses (torcula, at internal occipital protuberance)
  • → transverse sinuses
  • → sigmoid sinuses
  • → IJV (at jugular foramen).
  • Inferior sagittal sinus (free edge of falx) + great cerebral vein → straight sinus → confluence.
  • Cavernous sinuses (either side of sella; contain ICA, CN VI; lateral wall: III, IV, V1, V2) drain via superior and inferior petrosal sinuses
  • Receive ophthalmic veins (face connection).
  • Occipital sinus.
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST)
  • Risk factors: pregnancy/puerperium, combined oral contraceptive, thrombophilia, dehydration, malignancy, infection (mastoiditis → sigmoid/transverse; facial infection → cavernous sinus), head injury, IBD, (vaccine-induced thrombocytopenia).
  • Symptoms/signs: headache (progressive, worse lying down; can be thunderclap), signs of raised ICP (papilloedema, vomiting, diplopia from VI palsy), seizures (focal/generalised), focal deficits (venous infarcts, often haemorrhagic, not respecting arterial territories; bilateral with superior sagittal sinus), ↓ consciousness/encephalopathy (deep veins). Cavernous sinus thrombosis: proptosis, chemosis, periorbital oedema, ophthalmoplegia (III, IV, VI), V1/V2 sensory loss, fever.
  • Ix: CT venogram or MR venogram (empty delta sign on contrast CT); D-dimer not reliable.
  • Rx: anticoagulation (LMWH then oral anticoagulant, even if haemorrhagic infarcts), treat cause (antibiotics for septic), manage ICP/seizures; endovascular therapy if deteriorating.

los.text: Explain how the structure of the venous sinuses contribute to the development of subdural haemorrhage, particularly with relevance to the lucid interval.
los.html:
Subdural space
  • Potential space between the dura and arachnoid
  • Bridging (superior cerebral) veins cross it from the cortical surface to drain into the dural venous sinuses (especially superior sagittal sinus)
  • They are thin-walled and tethered at the sinus.
Mechanism
  • Acceleration–deceleration (shearing)
  • → brain moves relative to fixed dura/sinuses
  • → bridging veins tear
  • → venous bleeding into subdural space (low pressure → slow accumulation).
Risk factors
  • Brain atrophy (elderly, alcohol misuse, dementia) stretches the bridging veins and leaves more space → minor trauma (often forgotten) is enough
  • Anticoagulants/antiplatelets, coagulopathy, falls, infants (shaking injury: abusive head trauma), CSF overdrainage (shunts).
Acute subduralHigh-energy trauma, often with brain injury; rapid ↓ GCS; poor prognosis.
Chronic subdural
  • Develops over weeks
  • Collection enlarges (repeated microbleeds from neomembranes, osmotic/inflammatory processes) → insidious headache, confusion, drowsiness, personality change, unsteadiness, focal weakness, fluctuating consciousness.
"Lucid interval"
  • a period of apparent recovery after injury before deterioration.
  • Classically with extradural haematoma (arterial: hours), but subdural haematomas can also show a lucid/latent interval (venous: slow, days–weeks before symptoms) because there is space to fill (especially atrophic brains) before ICP rises.
RxChronic → burr-hole drainage (± MMA embolisation), stop/reverse anticoagulation; acute with mass effect → craniotomy.

los.text: Differentiate between subdural and extradural haemorrhage based on appearance and location on radiographs.
los.html:
Extradural haematomaSubdural haematoma
LocationBetween skull and dura (outer layer stripped)Between dura and arachnoid
ShapeBiconvex/lentiform (lens)Crescentic, concave inner margin following brain surface
SuturesDoes not cross sutures (dura firmly attached at sutures)Crosses sutures
MidlineCan cross midline (falx/sinus attachments allow)Does not cross midline (limited by falx) and doesn't extend into posterior fossa across tentorium (can layer along it)
SourceArterial (middle meningeal artery) ± venous sinusVenous (bridging veins)
AssociatedSkull fracture (temporal/pterion) in ~90%Brain atrophy, anticoagulation; underlying contusions (acute)
DensityAcute: hyperdense; may have swirl signAcute hyperdense; subacute isodense; chronic hypodense; acute-on-chronic mixed
Typical patientYoung adult, trauma, lucid intervalElderly/alcohol (chronic), high-energy trauma (acute)
  • Both cause mass effect (sulcal effacement, ventricular compression, midline shift) → neurosurgical emergency if significant.
